candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.8050 probability of malware, and all 20 listed n-grams push toward cryptojacking. However, the evidence is limited. No function names, API calls, or per-function locations were provided, so none of the n-grams can be tied to a specific routine such as a hashing loop. Every n-gram has a very low relative frequency (0.000104 to 0.001558), and individual SHAP contributions are small and spread out. The largest are DEC SBB (+0.020248) and SETA TEST (+0.017768), and the rest fall between +0.0054 and +0.0089. No single feature dominates. The patterns are mostly compiler-generated or generic integer-arithmetic idioms: conditional moves (CMOVC, CMOVNZ, CMOVLE, MOVZX CMOVL), SETcc flag materialization (SETA TEST, SETA OR, SETA XOR), sign and zero extensions (MOVZX, MOVSX, MOVSXD), and carry or borrow arithmetic (DEC SBB). Such code can occur in multi-precision arithmetic, hashing, or bit manipulation, which would be consistent with cryptographic or mining computation. It also appears routinely in benign code like runtime libraries, compression, parsing, and math routines. The n-grams MOVZX BTS, XOR DIV, and CDQ SUB hint at bit-level and division arithmetic, but they are not specific to mining. The classifier's probability favors malware, but the evidence cannot separate cryptojacking from ordinary arithmetic-heavy code. This supports a low-confidence tier rather than high-confidence.

evidence_analysis.assessment: The top contributor. DEC followed by SBB is a borrow/carry idiom often seen in multi-precision arithmetic or branchless masking. It is consistent with big-number or hash computation but also common in compiler output. Alone it is not diagnostic.

Materializes an unsigned-above condition into a byte and then tests it. This is a branchless comparison pattern. It is the second-strongest signal and the most frequent of the top few (0.000831), but it is generic.
Zero-extended load followed by a signed conditional move suggests branchless clamping or selection logic. It is plausible in data-processing loops and is non-specific.
A carry-conditional move followed by 32-to-64-bit sign extension. This is typical of 64-bit arithmetic and indexing code and only weakly suggestive of crypto routines.
Addition followed by a branch on sign flag. This is a common loop or bounds-check idiom with little cryptojacking specificity.
Another SETA flag-materialization pattern combined into a bitmask. Together with the other SETA n-grams it suggests a recurring branchless comparison style.
Address computation followed by a conditional branch. This is generic loop control and low specificity.
Sign extension of EAX into EDX followed by subtraction, typical of signed integer or division preparation. It is generic arithmetic.
An SSE unaligned move followed by a branch. It indicates vectorized memory copying or processing, which is common in benign runtime code and only weakly relevant to mining.
Zero-extension followed by bit-test-and-set indicates bitfield or bitmap manipulation. It could relate to bit-level algorithms, but it is also used in benign bitset and allocator code.
Condition materialization combined with XOR. This is a third SETA variant, suggesting a consistent compiler or code style. XOR is common in hashing but is not conclusive here.
A conditional move followed by a right shift is a branchless arithmetic or bit-manipulation pattern. It is weakly consistent with hashing-style code.
Zero-extension followed by negation is typical of masking or absolute-value computations. It is generic.

This is the most frequent n-gram in the list (0.001558). It is a counter increment followed by a conditional move, typical of branchless loop or selection logic. Its high frequency suggests a common compiler idiom.
Subtraction followed by sign extension, typical of narrow integer arithmetic. It is non-specific.
A frequent arithmetic and address-generation sequence (0.001454). It is ubiquitous in compiled code and contributes little specific evidence.
Addition followed by masking is common in modular arithmetic and hashing, but it is also widespread in benign code.
Negation followed by comparison, typical of signed comparison or absolute-value logic. It is generic.
A signed conditional move followed by addition indicates branchless min/max or clamping arithmetic. It is generic.
XOR (typically zeroing EDX) before DIV is the standard unsigned-division setup. Division and modulo appear in some hashing and mining code but also in ordinary code, so it is not discriminating.
